cards.title: DeepSeek Harness Desktop for macOS and Windows

depth.text: DeepSeek has a **desktop app** where you can **build plugins** by chatting with its AI

It’s in **public preview worldwide** and open source, with desktop downloads for macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows (64-bit). Users can install plugins or **create them through chat** in “Creator mode”; the page says core plugins and APIs are evolving.

cards.camps: Two camps: fans see the “everything is a plugin” design as a big strength; skeptics question the need for another harness and worry about third-party plugins or lock-in.

comments.text: Is this cheaper or better then just using openrouter and every other harness / tui out there?

My problem with plugins is that I don't want to install stuff from third parties. It might be malware, become unsupported, or generally have a lower quality. I rather have a curated and polished feature set out of the box. It's nice for having your AI create your own plugins. But I haven't really found the need yet.

This page doesn't emphasize the cordis architecture [1], but that's the most exciting thing about this -- not just yet another harness. It has the potential to make this into something like the emacs of harnesses! I think this might be particularly potent for long-running agents. [1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25512

Why does every lab producing an LLM want to have their own harness? Lock-in? Is there any other advantage for the lab? I'm using Cursor (it's the only way my company allows us to use Grok) and OpenChamber (when using GPT, Muse Spark and others) and I'm happy. If I were to use DeepSeek, I'd use it through OpenChamber too. * OpenChamber is a GUI for OpenCode.

https://frontierharness.org/ allegedly this is on the Pareto frontier, though I don't know how good of a benchmark this really is. it seems to focus on one-shot type tasks, whereas the real utility of one harness over another seems to make itself known in long running tasks. also this is a very limited static snapshot with one model as backend, I wish there were more consistently refreshed and…

The comments describe it as a **pastiche** of Arnold Lobel's “Frog and Toad” books. Another commenter worries the children's-story framing can make machine motives seem **too human**; a reader says it helped explain the breach.

cards.camps: Some praise it as funny and illuminating; others worry the portrayal misleads or raise concerns about borrowing Lobel's style.

comments.text:
Frog put the AI in a sandbox. "There." he said. "Now it will not hack
any more companies." "But it can escape the sandbox."
said Toad. "That is true." said Frog.

Someone who read some hype article about how competent and clever openai for making a bad sandbox is could read this and immediately understand that it was entirely their own fault.

cards.title: How Singapore's government-run dating service works

depth.text: Singapore is testing **FirstDate**, but the writer doubts an algorithm can create **chemistry**

FirstDate uses Singpass to verify users, then offers **one match each cycle** and shares contact details only if both people agree. Its questionnaire has **over 30 questions**; the writer says the preference checklist keeps dating transactional and proposes funding **culture clubs**, theatre groups, video game conventions and music festivals instead.

cards.camps: Two camps: skeptics say dating is too messy for algorithms; defenders say a government service can still beat commercial apps and offer better-than-random matches.

comments.text: You know, there's probably fewer perverse incentives with a government run dating service. Obviously I can imagine ways it could suck, but when I compare them to how commercial dating services are run it's hard to see how they could do a _worse_ job.

I think this would be better than commercial services, which have all the wrong incentives. I would think just a coarse sorting would do, paired with a free meal. Every couple of weeks, you go for a random date with a somewhat well paired person, and see what happens. Maybe you don't meet the love of your life, but you will meet someone roughly your age living in the same society, a perspective…

Gale-Shapley, used in this service, has the property that one side ("proposing" side) is guaranteed their most advantageous stable match while the other side is guaranteed their worst possible stable match. I've never heard this discussed or mentioned as a drawback because it's Nobel Prize winning and "stable" is a shorthand for "fair". Even though there's many unique stable matches that each…

If women were (legally allowed and required ) to be paid upfront for delivering and raising children, the market would sort things out. We would probably get some professional mothers who would have 6-12 children.

> In short, stable matches mean nothing when nobody is committed and the best options might exist outside of the matchmaking pool This is wrong. Stable matches still mean something , and in fact probably mean quite a lot. You are given a much better match than a random pairing. If you still aren't interested, you can decline. If you go on a date and it doesn't work out, you can decline. Nothing…

cards.title: Context Language Models

depth.text: someone gave language models a way to **manage their own context** by **editing a file**

The paper treats context as a file the model can **update freely**, then reports better results with less compute on several tasks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it reports **11.4% higher accuracy** with **21.5% fewer FLOPs**; its online reinforcement-learning method improved Qwen3.5-9B performance by 47.6% while using 12% fewer FLOPs.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters call this a promising answer to a major LLM hassle; skeptics worry context upkeep uses attention and causes cache misses, and prefer a separate agent.

comments.text: Letting a model manage its own context is very bitter lesson-pilled Biggest challenge is you will get a much lower cache hit rate if you frequently edit the agent's context/prefix, so this can not be implemented efficiently via e.g. the Anthropic API. This ^ can be solved in principle but likely requires modifications to the transformer architecture and definitely to serving infrastructure See…

I would be concerned with context management consuming limited attention resources. Do you want your agent solving its own memory crisis, or do you want it solving the actual task? It can probably do both at the same time, but I suspect there is a non trivial cost associated with this. A separate hypervisor agent that manages the main agent's context would be much better in my experience. You can…
The biggest discovery might actually be that they ignored regular caching rules and kept invalid cache suffixes and it didn't hurt performance

Wow. Context management is one of the big remaining hassles with modern LLMs so this could be big. The obvious complication is cache busting so it's also exciting they investigated solutions for that.
Related: "Recursive Language Models" https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24601

So we're looking at a massively accelerated volume of security vulnerabilities for the foreseeable future thanks to AI-assisted security research, and we can expect no reduction in new vulnerabilities from the AIs…

cards.title: Various Projects Find Hidden SDR Capabilities in ESP32 Microcontrollers

depth.text: someone found a **hidden feature** that lets ESP32 chips capture **raw radio signals**, beyond WiFi and Bluetooth

Several models can capture raw IQ samples across **2.2–2.7 GHz**, with the ESP32-C5 also covering **4.8–6.0 GHz**. For general PC use, most can only export snapshots, but the ESP32-S31 can stream continuously at up to **16 MS/s** over Gigabit Ethernet.

cards.title: Automatic Transmission – a data-privacy study of connected vehicles

depth.text: a study found **connected cars** and their apps sending **personal data** to outside companies

Researchers tested **21 vehicles** and **30 companion apps**: 19 vehicles contacted at least one third party over Wi-Fi, and seven apps sent sensitive identifiers to third parties. Pairing an app **roughly doubled** exposure to advertising and tracking companies on average.
data: vehicles contacting a third party over Wi-Fi

cards.camps: Two camps: one commenter says owners can simply stop using connected-vehicle features; another says cars still send telemetry and opting out can be hard or impossible.

comments.text: I currently drive a mid 2000s Ford truck, which runs great and meets my needs, but lately I got interested in minivans/people carriers. I pretty quickly realized that newer vehicles seem to not just record, but export a lot of driving data. The minivan market is small. There are really only 4-5 available and every single one sends telemetry data from the car and makes it hard/impossible to opt…

if an owner decides they are uncomfortable with the data sharing described within them, they are faced with (arguably) unfair choices:
- 01 accept the agreements regardless of their concerns
- 02 stop using their car's connected-vehicle features - which includes remote start, the app, and other very useful features
- 03 stop using the vehicle entirely
Easy, I take #2. Is that it? This whole time…
> As one notable exception, Honda improved its data collection practices to prevent sending precise geolocation to a third party associated with user tracking. I know what my next car will be.

The ongoing theme of all these responses was shifting the blame to the consumer. As expected. I think consumers also need to push back on these practices, but the problem is, majority of consumers are tech savy but not privacy savy.

Hope to see a new market for disabling telemetry and phonehome features from cars. It should be legal to do so, if you own the car I suppose. I'm thinking that rigth now few pople even know how much spying their new car does to them but this will change and as awareness grows more and more people will want to do it.

glossary.harness: The surrounding code that gives an AI agent tools and a place to work, and checks what it does.
glossary.plugin: An add-on that gives an app extra tools or features.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.Cordis: The architecture DeepSeek Harness is built on; its pitch is that everything in the system is a plugin.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.anthropomorphism: Describing something nonhuman as if it had human thoughts or feelings.
glossary.pastiche: A work that imitates the style of another work or creator.
glossary.persistent: Here, it can mean lasting, or continuing to try; commenters debate which meaning was intended.
glossary.Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage Algorithm: A method for pairing two groups by their choices, where no two people would both prefer each other over their assigned partners.
glossary.stable match: A pairing where no two people would both rather be with each other than with their assigned partners.
glossary.Singpass: Singapore's service for confirming a user's identity online.
glossary.third spaces: Places outside home and work where people can spend time and meet others, like clubs or cafés.
glossary.BTO: Build-To-Order: Singapore's public-housing system, which the article says can shape couples' plans around housing.
glossary.algorithm: A set of steps used to solve a problem or make a decision.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.subagent: A helper assigned a smaller part of a larger task.
glossary.Turing test: A test where someone chats with a computer and tries to tell whether it’s a person.
glossary.ASCII art: Pictures made from ordinary text characters like letters and punctuation.
glossary.freewheel: A bike part that lets the wheel keep turning while you stop pedaling.
glossary.rear mech: The part by the back wheel that moves the chain between gears.
glossary.groupset: A collection of bike parts used to change gears and control the brakes.
glossary.peloton: The main group of riders in a bicycle race.
glossary.CLM: Context Language Model: a language model that manages its own context, including by changing a file of information it keeps available.
glossary.FLOPs: Floating-point operations: a count of computer math steps, used here as a measure of how much compute a run takes.
glossary.cache hit rate: How often a system can reuse saved work instead of calculating it again.
glossary.reinforcement learning: A way to train an AI by rewarding choices that work and discouraging choices that do not.
glossary.Racket: A programming language used to build software and experiment with language design.
glossary.Rhombus: A programming language in the Racket family that can be used to build new language features.
glossary.macro: A tool that lets programmers add language features or transform code before it runs.
glossary.compiler: A tool that turns code you write into a program a computer can run.
glossary.floating-point: A way computers store numbers with decimal parts, which can introduce rounding errors.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a standard ID assigned to a publicly known security flaw so people can refer to the same issue.
glossary.privilege escalation: A flaw that lets someone get more control of a computer than they should have.
glossary.denial of service: An attack or flaw that makes a service unavailable to people trying to use it.
glossary.kernel: A small program that carries out a calculation on a computer's graphics chip or processor.
glossary.framework: A collection of ready-made parts and rules that helps people build software.
glossary.type safety: Checks that values are used in ways the code expects, catching some mistakes before the app runs.
glossary.migration: Changing code to work with a newer version, sometimes with steps handled automatically.
glossary.alias: A shorter stand-in name for a longer file path.
glossary.remote functions: Tools for letting an app safely send work to a server and get an answer back.
glossary.Async Svelte: A Svelte capability that remote functions need, and that currently has to be switched on experimentally.
glossary.experimental flag: A setting you turn on to try a feature that isn't ready for ordinary use.
glossary.SDR: Software-defined radio: a radio that uses software to handle signals instead of being limited to one fixed radio function.
glossary.IQ samples: A pair of measurements that records a radio signal’s strength and position in its wave, so software can process it.
glossary.GHz: Gigahertz: a unit for how quickly a radio wave repeats.
glossary.MS/s: Millions of samples per second; it describes how quickly the device captures measurements of a signal.
glossary.GenAI: Generative AI: tools that make new text, images, or code from instructions.
glossary.LLMs: Large language models: computer programs trained on lots of writing that can produce text.
glossary.Developer Relations: A company role focused on helping developers learn about and use its products.
glossary.API reference: A guide to the ways a program can ask another program for information or actions.
glossary.AI crawlers: Automated programs that visit websites and collect their content for AI systems.
glossary.nondeterministic: Able to give different results even when asked the same thing twice.
glossary.agentic: Describes AI that chooses steps and acts toward a task, rather than only answering a question.
glossary.full-stack: Building both the parts of an app people use and the behind-the-scenes parts that make it work.
glossary.Revenue Cycle Management (RCM): The steps a healthcare provider takes to check coverage, bill for care, and collect payment.
glossary.connected vehicle: A car with internet access that can keep communicating with its maker and other companies.
glossary.third party: A company outside the carmaker that receives information from the car or its app.
glossary.telemetry: Information a program sends back about how it is being used or whether it is working properly.
glossary.sensitive identifiers: Personal details that can point to someone or their vehicle, such as an email, phone number, or vehicle ID.
glossary.VIN: Vehicle Identification Number: a number that identifies a particular vehicle.
glossary.Faraday tent: A tent that blocks radio signals; researchers used one to cut off the cars' cellular connections.
glossary.PII: Personally Identifiable Information: details that could identify someone, such as an email or phone number.
